plan.topic_summary: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks from quantum computers. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is how quickly and reliably organizations can migrate from current public-key schemes to PQC, what performance and operational tradeoffs that migration introduces, and how the pace of quantum-computing progress shapes the urgency of adoption.
key_questions: What is the current state of PQC standardization (NIST and international bodies) and which algorithm families are finalized or near-final?
What measurable performance overhead (latency, bandwidth, key size, compute) do PQC algorithms introduce in TLS, IoT, and cloud workloads compared to classical equivalents?
How are major cloud providers, financial institutions, and governments structuring their PQC migration roadmaps, and what are the primary blockers?
What implementation-level vulnerabilities (side channels, fault injection, software bugs) have been demonstrated in PQC, and how do they compare to classical crypto risk?
What is the realistic timeline for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer, and how does that uncertainty affect the cost-benefit calculus of early PQC adoption?
Will hybrid (classical + PQC) schemes become the dominant deployment model, and what are the long-term implications for cryptographic agility and key management infrastructure?

gaps: No specific quantitative performance overhead figures (e.g., key size ratios, throughput degradation percentages) are extracted in the findings, though the underlying papers likely contain them
Quantum computer timeline estimates are absent; the report will need to frame urgency without a grounded 'Q-day' date

Code-based and multivariate cryptography families are mentioned only in passing (S7) with no dedicated performance or security analysis, though this is less critical given lattice-based dominance in NIST standards
X4 market size projection ($0.6B to $3.8B by 2031) is a single unverified social signal with no corroboration from filings or papers

sources.title: Post-quantum Cryptography
Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures
sources.venue: Gillot, O., Buchanan, W. J., & Tehrani, M. G. (2026). Energy Consumption of Post-Quantum Cryptography on Constrained and General-Purpose Architectures. Cryptography, 10(4), 55
sources.abstract: With Q-day approaching, the transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has begun, with governments across the US, UK and EU mandating migration to quantum-resistant standards. This paper benchmarks the three NIST-standardised PQC algorithms - FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) - across key generation, signing and verification operations, measuring both computational performance and energy consumption on a range of constrained IoT-class devices, from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL~3.5, results show that ML-KEM and ML-DSA achieve energy and speed efficiency comparable to classical elliptic-curve cryptography across all tested architectures. However, SLH-DSA signing is inadvisable on constrained hardware: energy costs for SLH-DSA signing on 32-bit devices were up to 243\% higher than on equivalent 64-bit hardware, making it impractical for resource-limited IoT deployments. These findings have direct implications for IoT security practitioners planning PQC migration.

sources.title: A Survey of Post-Quantum Cryptography: Start of a New Race
sources.abstract: Information security is a fundamental and urgent issue in the digital transformation era. Cryptographic techniques and digital signatures have been applied to protect and authenticate relevant information. However, with the advent of quantum computers and quantum algorithms, classical cryptographic techniques have been in danger of collapsing because quantum computers can solve complex problems in polynomial time. Stemming from that risk, researchers worldwide have stepped up research on post-quantum algorithms to resist attack by quantum computers. In this review paper, we survey studies in recent years on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and provide statistics on the number and content of publications, including a literature overview, detailed explanations of the most common methods so far, current implementation status, implementation comparisons, and discussion on future work. These studies focused on essential public cryptography techniques and digital signature schemes, and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) launched a competition to select the best candidate for the expected standard. Recent studies have practically implemented the public key encryption/key encapsulation mechanism (PKE/KEM) and digital signature schemes on different hardware platforms and applied various optimization measures based on other criteria. Along with the increasing number of scientific publications, the recent trend of PQC research is increasingly evident and is the general trend in the cryptography industry. The movement opens up a promising avenue for researchers in public key cryptography and digital signatures, especially on algorithms selected by NIST.

sources.title: A Comparative Performance Evaluation of Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM for Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) aims to develop cryptographic algorithms that are secure against attacks from quantum computers. This paper compares the leading postquantum cryptographic algorithms, such as Kyber, sntrup761, and FrodoKEM, in terms of their security, performance, and real-world applicability. The review highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm and provides insights into future research directions. We also discuss the challenges of transitioning from classical to post-quantum systems and the potential impacts on various industries. This paper serves as a foundation for understanding the current state of post-quantum cryptography and its future prospects in the quantum computing era.

sources.title: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
A Survey on Post-Quantum Cryptography: State-of-the-Art and Challenges
sources.abstract: The paper explains that post-quantum cryptography is necessary due to the introduction of quantum computing causing certain algorithms to be broken. We analyze the different types of post-quantum cryptography, quantum cryptography and quantum-resistant cryptography, to provide a thorough understanding of the current solutions to the problems and their limitations. We explain the current state of quantum computing and how it has changed over time while discussing possible attacks on both types of post-quantum cryptography. Next, current post-quantum algorithms are discussed, and implementations are demonstrated. Lastly, we conclude that due to quantum cryptography's present limitations it is not a viable solution like it is often presented to be and that it is currently better to use quantum-resistant cryptography.

sources.title: Post Quantum Cryptography: A Review of Techniques, Challenges and Standardizations
sources.abstract: The development of large quantum computers will have dire consequences for cryptography. Most of the symmetric and asymmetric cryptographic algorithms are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. Grover’s search algorithm gives a square root time boost for the searching of the key in symmetric schemes like AES and 3DES. The security of asymmetric algorithms like RSA, Diffie Hellman, and ECC is based on the mathematical hardness of prime factorization and discrete logarithms. The best classical algorithms available take exponential time. Shor’s factoring algorithm can solve the problems in polynomial time. Major breakthroughs in quantum computing will render all the present-day widely used asymmetric cryptosystems insecure. This paper analyzes the vulnerability of the classical cryptosystems in the context of quantum computers, discusses various post-quantum cryptosystem families, discusses the status of the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization process, provides a performance comparison of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms on different platforms, and finally provides a couple of future research directions in this field.

sources.title: The Mathematical Foundation of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: On July 5, 2022, the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced four possible post-quantum cryptography standards, three of them are based on lattice theory and the other one is based on Hash function. It is well-known that the security of the lattice cryptography relies on the hardness of the shortest vector problem (SVP) and the closest vector problem (CVP). In fact, the SVP is a sphere packing problem and the CVP is a sphere covering problem. Furthermore, both SVP and CVP are equivalent to arithmetic problems of positive definite quadratic forms. This paper will briefly introduce the post-quantum cryptography and show its connections with sphere packing, sphere covering, and positive definite quadratic forms.

sources.title: Post-quantum cryptography and the quantum future of cybersecurity
sources.abstract: We review the current status of efforts to develop and deploy post-quantum cryptography on the Internet. Then we suggest specific ways in which quantum technologies might be used to enhance cybersecurity in the near future and beyond. We focus on two goals: protecting the secret keys that are used in classical cryptography, and ensuring the trustworthiness of quantum computations. These goals may soon be within reach, thanks to recent progress in both theory and experiment. This progress includes interactive protocols for testing quantumness as well as for performing uncloneable cryptographic computations; and experimental demonstrations of device-independent random number generators, device-independent quantum key distribution, quantum memories, and analog quantum simulators.

sources.title: Obfuscated Quantum and Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC) 2026 Kobe, Japan
sources.abstract: In this work, we present an experimental deployment of a new design for combined quantum key distribution (QKD) and post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Novel to our system is the dynamic obfuscation of the QKD-PQC sequence of operations, the number of operations, and parameters related to the operations; coupled to the integration of a GPS-free quantum synchronization protocol within the QKD process. We compare the performance and overhead of our QKD-PQC system relative to a standard QKD system with one-time pad encryption, demonstrating that our design can operate in real time with little additional overhead caused by the new security features. Since our system can offer additional defensive strategies against a wide spectrum of practical attacks that undermine deployed QKD, PQC, and certain combinations of these two primitives, we suggest that our design represents one of the most secure communication systems currently available. Given the dynamic nature of its obfuscation attributes, our new system can also be adapted in the field to defeat yet-to-be-discovered practical attacks.

sources.title: Applications of Post-Quantum Cryptography
sources.venue: European Conference on Cyber Warfare and Security
sources.abstract: With the constantly advancing capabilities of quantum computers, conventional cryptographic systems relying on complex math problems may encounter unforeseen vulnerabilities. Unlike regular computers, which are often deemed cost-ineffective in cryptographic attacks, quantum computers have a significant advantage in calculation speed. This distinction potentially makes currently used algorithms less secure or even completely vulnerable, compelling the exploration of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) as the most reasonable solution to quantum threats. This review aims to provide current information on applications, benefits, and challenges associated with the PQC. The review employs a systematic scoping review with the scope restricted to the years 2022 and 2023; only articles that were published in scientific journals were used in this paper. The review examined the articles on the applications of quantum computing in various spheres. However, the scope of this paper was restricted to the domain of the PQC because most of the analyzed articles featured this field. Subsequently, the paper is analyzing various PQC algorithms, including lattice-based, hash-based, code-based, multivariate polynomial, and isogeny-based cryptography. Each algorithm is being judged based on its potential applications, robustness, and challenges. All the analyzed algorithms are promising for the post-quantum era in such applications as digital signatures, communication channels, and IoT. Moreover, some of the algorithms are already implemented in the spheres of banking transactions, communication, and intellectual property. Meanwhile, despite their potential, these algorithms face serious challenges since they lack standardization, require vast amounts of storage and computation power, and might have unknown vulnerabilities that can be discovered only with years of cryptanalysis. This overview aims to give a basic understanding of the current state of post-quantum cryptography with its applications and challenges. As the world enters the quantum era, this review not only shows the need for strong security methods that can resist quantum attacks but also presents an optimistic outlook on the future of secure communications, guided by advancements in quantum technology. By bridging the gap between theoretical research and practical implementation, this paper aims to inspire further innovation and collaboration in the field.

sources.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Neural Network
sources.abstract: In recent years, quantum computers and Shor quantum algorithm have posed a threat to current mainstream asymmetric cryptography methods (e.g. RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)). Therefore, it is necessary to construct a Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) method to resist quantum computing attacks. Therefore, this study proposes a PQC-based neural network that maps a code-based PQC method to a neural network structure and enhances the security of ciphertexts with non-linear activation functions, random perturbation of ciphertexts, and uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In practical experiments, this study uses cellular network signals as a case study to demonstrate that encryption and decryption can be performed by the proposed PQC-based neural network with the uniform distribution of ciphertexts. In the future, the proposed PQC-based neural network could be applied to various applications.

sources.title: A closer look at the belief propagation algorithm in side-channel attack on CCA-secure PQC KEM
Invited Paper: Machine Learning Based Blind Side-Channel Attacks on PQC-Based KEMs - A Case Study of Kyber KEM
sources.abstract: Kyber KEM, the NIST selected PQC standard for Public Key Encryption and Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) has been subjected to a variety of side-channel attacks, through the course of the NIST PQC standardization process. However, all these attacks targeting the decapsulation procedure of Kyber KEM either require knowledge of the ciphertexts or require to control the value of ciphertexts for key recovery. However, there are no known attacks in a blind setting, where the attacker does not have access to the ciphertexts. While blind side-channel attacks are known for symmetric key cryptographic schemes, we are not aware of such attacks for Kyber KEM. In this paper, we fill this gap by proposing the first blind side-channel attack on Kyber KEM. We target leakage of the pointwise multiplication operation in the decryption procedure to carry out practical blind side-channel attacks resulting in full key recovery. We perform practical validation of our attack using power side-channel from the reference implementation of Kyber KEM taken from the pqm4 library, implemented on the ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller. Our experiments clearly indicate the feasibility of our proposed attack in recovering the full key in only a few hundred to few thousand traces, in the presence of a suitably accurate Hamming Weight (HW) classifier.

sources.title: Hardware Design for Decomposition Module with Variable-Order Masking against Side-Channel Attack for PQC ML-DSA
sources.venue: International Conference on Integrated Circuits and Microsystems (ICICM)
sources.abstract: In terms of encryption protection, the hardware optimization implementation of the ML-DSA basic decomposition core is truly revolutionary, specifically designed to counter the new threat of quantum computing. We replaced modular arithmetic and conditional branches with bitwise lookup operations, which stabilized execution time and resolved control flow leakage issues. Additionally, a dynamic Boolean masking framework enables the module to defend against first-order and higher-order side-channel attacks as needed, without affecting processing speed. This accelerator is written in Verilog and implemented on a Xilinx FPGA, with a critical path delay of only 0.534 ns and a pure logic propagation delay of just 0.003 ns, outperforming both branch-based (1.804 ns) and modular (0.739 ns) solutions. We also conducted comprehensive static timing analysis and theoretical side-channel assessments, both of which confirmed no temporal asymmetry, meaning this module is particularly effective in secure lattice-based environments. These findings demonstrate that the proposed architecture can serve as a high-performance, side-channel-resistant engine for nextgeneration post-quantum signature frameworks.

sources.title: SoK: Reassessing Side-Channel Vulnerabilities and Countermeasures in PQC Implementations
sources.venue: ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security (ASIA CCS)
sources.abstract: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) algorithms should remain secure even in the presence of quantum computers. Although the security of such schemes is guaranteed at the algorithmic level, real-world implementations often suffer from other vulnerabilities like Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) attacks. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) paper investigates SCA attacks targeting implementations of PQC algorithms. This work categorizes attacks from an adversarial perspective to identify the most vulnerable components of the algorithms' implementations and highlights unexplored parts in current implementations. In addition, it reviews and analyzes the efficiency and efficacy of existing countermeasures to SCA attacks in current hardware implementations. This approach helps identify countermeasures that provide broader protection and highlights characteristics needed for future secure implementations. Our findings offer guidance in strengthening existing systems and developing more efficient defenses against side-channel attacks.

sources.title: Balancing Quantum and Classical Security: Side-Channel Challenges in NIST PQC Finalist
sources.venue: International Conference on Sustainable Computing and Data Communication Systems (ICSCDS)
sources.abstract: As quantum computing presents a known threat to classical cryptographic systems, the design of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) has been essential. Although NIST PQC finalists are specifically designed to resist quantum attacks, their susceptibility to side-channel attacks (SCAs) is still an important issue. This work analyzes the susceptibility of lattice-based, code-based, and hash-based PQC schemes against SCAs, such as power analysis, timing attacks, and fault injection. Lattice-based schemes are vulnerable to power attacks and fault injections, whereas code-based schemes are vulnerable to timing attacks. Most SCAs are mitigated in hash-based schemes however they are prone to a fault injection attack. Various countermeasures including masking, constant-time computation, and fault detection techniques are discussed, with their strengths and performance penalty emphasized. Some of the identified challenges include the lack of hardware agnostic countermeasures, hardware specific vulnerabilities. The future research directions are calling for efficient, hardware-agnostic standards to establish the practical security of PQC algorithms. Successfully overcoming such challenges ensures that the transition to PQC will not need to sacrifice resistance to both quantum and classical attacks.

sources.title: Exploring Side-Channel Protections in Hardware Implementations of PQC ML-KEM Verification
sources.abstract: As ML-KEM is adopted as a post-quantum cryptographic standard, resilience against physical side-channel attacks has become essential. Among the constituent steps, the decapsulation Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) verification is particularly vulnerable to side-channel power and electromagnetic (EM) analysis. In this work, we focus on common FPGA-based implementations and examine their side-channel vulnerabilities, and compare them with those of microcontroller implementations. Three verification implementations, unprotected, hash-based (first-order), and higher-order masked, are evaluated for side-channel security on both a microcontroller and an FPGA. While FPGAs offer higher speed and parallelism, they often exhibit stronger side-channel leakage, especially in high bandwidth configurations. The higher-order masked designs still leak information about the underlying data due to hardware-level effects and data-dependent processing. Our experiments show that their parallelized processing on FPGAs introduces sufficient first-order leakage for full secret-key recovery. These results underscore the persistent challenge of securing PQC algorithms in performance-constrained and parallelized hardware environments.

sources.title: A Look at Side Channel Attacks on Post-quantum Cryptography
sources.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is designed to be secure against attacks from quantum computers, yet it remains vulnerable to classic side-channel attacks (SCAs), which exploit physical implementation leaks. This manuscript examines the various SCAs used to evaluate PQC schemes, focusing on non-invasive techniques such as timing, power, and electromagnetic analysis. We provide a detailed account of the execution of these attacks against diverse PQC algorithms and identify common vulnerabilities and weaknesses. Our study reveals that, while various countermeasures have been proposed to protect PQC implementations, they are not entirely effective against sophisticated attacks. Stronger and more resilient countermeasures are needed, especially in IoT environments. The review highlights the weaknesses in the current defenses, including the necessity for more robust masking techniques, adequate security countermeasures tailored to IoT constraints, and methods to generalize SCAs across diverse hardware platforms. These issues must be addressed to enhance the practical security of PQC schemes in real-world scenarios.

sources.title: Roadmap of post-quantum cryptography standardization: Side-channel attacks and countermeasures
Multiple-Valued Plaintext-Checking Side-Channel Attacks on Post-Quantum KEMs
sources.venue: IACR Transactions on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems
sources.abstract: In this paper, we present a side-channel analysis (SCA) on key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) based on the Fujisaki–Okamoto (FO) transformation and its variants. Many post-quantum KEMs usually perform re-encryption during key decapsulation to achieve chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) security. The side-channel leakage of re-encryption can be exploited to mount a key-recovery plaintext-checking attack (KR-PCA), even if the chosen-plaintext attack (CCA) secure decryption constructing the KEM is securely implemented. Herein, we propose an efficient side-channel-assisted KR-PCA on post-quantum KEMs, and achieve a key recovery with significantly fewer attack traces than existing ones in TCHES 2022 and 2023. The basic concept of the proposed attack is to introduce a new KR-PCA based on a multiple-valued (MV-)PC oracle and then implement a dedicated MV-PC oracle based on a multi-classification neural network (NN). The proposed attack is applicable to the NIST PQC selected algorithm Kyber and the similar lattice-based Saber, FrodoKEM and NTRU Prime, as well as SIKE. We also present how to realize a sufficiently reliable MV-PC oracle from NN model outputs that are not 100% accurate, and analyze the tradeoff between the key recovery success rate and the number of attack traces. We assess the feasibility of the proposed attack through attack experiments on three typical symmetric primitives to instantiate a random oracle (SHAKE, SHA3, and AES software). The proposed attack reduces the number of attack traces required for a reliable key recovery by up to 87% compared to the existing attacks against Kyber and other lattice-based KEMs, under the condition of 99.9999% success rate for key recovery. The proposed attack can also reduce the number of attack traces by 85% for SIKE.

sources.title: Distill-and-Rank: Evaluating Fast Transformer Models for Keyless PQC Side-Channel Recovery
sources.venue: IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems (MWSCAS)
sources.abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) schemes such as the NIST-standardized ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber) are entering deployment, yet their resilience to side-channel attacks (SCAs) remains insufficiently understood. We study a realistic keyless attack on ML-KEM’s pointwise multiplication: a leakage model trained only on a disjoint known-key set recovers each target’s secret by ranking candidate coefficients without ever using its key, relying solely on the public ciphertext r and the traces. On low-noise simulated traces and real CW305 FPGA measurements, we recover the NTT-domain coefficients of $s_{1}$ and benchmark CPA, a 1-D CNN, and a compact hybrid (Reg-Net) against our Distill-and-Rank framework, which pairs PatchSCA-Lite, a lightweight patch-based Transformer (153k parameters, ~2 ms/trace), with EMA self-distillation, correlation ranking, and keyless confidence measures (margin, bootstrap stability). On low-noise traces all learned models beat CPA (25 traces to disclosure); the compact hybrid needs the fewest (12) and PatchSCA-Lite 17, with EMA distillation essential for the Transformer to converge. Under high noise and on real hardware, learned models degrade sharply: the compact hybrid gives the best efficiency-robustness tradeoff, while pure attention collapses where low SNR and scale mismatch dominate. Standardized PQC implementations remain vulnerable to leakage, and lightweight hybrid models are the more practical choice for keyless SCA.

sources.title: Fermion lattices can be simulated by same-size qubit lattices with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ interaction overhead
sources.abstract: Local interactions among electrons underlie many complex properties of correlated materials. While the Jordan-Wigner transformation can preserve this locality along one spatial dimension, interactions along the remaining dimensions typically incur substantial overhead. We show how to simulate all geometrically local interactions on an $N$-site two-dimensional fermion lattice with no asymptotic overhead in the number of interactions and no space overhead. The primary overhead of our method is circuit depth, which on a qubit lattice matches that of fermionic swap networks, scaling as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$, but reduces to $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ on reconfigurable qubit arrays and to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ in lattice-surgery-based surface-code architectures. This is enabled by dynamically reorienting the Jordan-Wigner transformation to switch the lattice dimension along which locality is preserved. Furthermore, we study fermion routing, as required for the simulation of non-local interactions. When using qubit lattices, we reach resource scaling that asymptotically matches that of qubit routing, whilst on fully connected qubit devices, a depth scaling arbitrarily close to $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ is reached. This allows the fermionic fast Fourier transform to be implemented on qubit lattices with asymptotically optimal resource scaling under these locality constraints. Notably, all of our constructions naturally extend to $d$-dimensional lattices. Beyond scaling improvements, we show explicit examples of our method, including Fermi-Hubbard-model simulations of the square-, Lieb- and kagome lattice and the fermionic fast Fourier transform.

findings.claim: Masked and protected hardware implementations of ML-KEM can still leak enough for full secret-key recovery. In the reported FPGA experiments, higher-order masking did not remove the leakage in the FO verification step.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This rests on one arXiv preprint, which is not peer reviewed, and on an abstract only. The result applies to the specific FPGA and microcontroller designs tested, so it may not carry over to other implementations. It does challenge the assumption that masking is a sufficient fix.
findings.supporting_excerpt: The higher-order masked designs still leak information about the underlying data due to hardware-level effects and data-dependent processing.

findings.claim: Side-channel attacks on the standardized Kyber/ML-KEM keep widening in scope. A blind attack that needs no ciphertext knowledge has been demonstrated, and neural-network-assisted plaintext-checking attacks cut the traces needed and apply across several lattice KEMs.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Two abstracts describe attacks on different parts of FO-based KEMs. The blind attack was validated on a pqm4 reference implementation on a Cortex-M4 with an assumed accurate Hamming Weight classifier. The plaintext-checking abstract is truncated, and its experiments cover software instantiations of SHAKE, SHA3 and AES. Both are lab demonstrations rather than field attacks. Attack success depends on attacker access to physical leakage.
findings.supporting_excerpt: we fill this gap by proposing the first blind side-channel attack on Kyber KEM.

findings.claim: Several reviews conclude that current side-channel countermeasures for PQC are incomplete. They are not fully effective against sophisticated attacks, are not hardware-agnostic, and are especially weak for constrained IoT devices.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Three independent review or SoK abstracts point the same way, but they are secondary syntheses. Their conclusions depend on which primary attacks they surveyed. The abstracts give no quantified performance penalties for the countermeasures.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Our study reveals that, while various countermeasures have been proposed to protect PQC implementations, they are not entirely effective against sophisticated attacks.

findings.claim: Hardware acceleration may worsen side-channel exposure. FPGA implementations, valued for speed and parallelism, showed stronger leakage than microcontroller implementations, especially in high-bandwidth configurations. This is a tension between performance and security.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The main evidence is one arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed) saying FPGAs 'often exhibit stronger side-channel leakage'. A review abstract adds that countermeasures are hardware-specific. This is my generalization across the two, and it may not hold for all FPGA or ASIC designs.

findings.claim: Evidence that ML-based attacks work is mostly from low-noise or simulated conditions. One study found learned models degrade sharply under high noise and on real hardware, which tempers worst-case claims, but that does not make the implementations safe.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single conference abstract. It shows real-hardware (CW305) recovery was still reported, but efficiency fell in noisy settings. The same abstract concludes that implementations remain vulnerable. It is a mixed signal on practical attack difficulty, so attack feasibility depends on measurement conditions.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Under high noise and on real hardware, learned models degrade sharply: the compact hybrid gives the best efficiency-robustness tradeoff, while pure attention collapses where low SNR and scale mismatch dominate.

findings.claim: Protection of the newer ML-DSA signature scheme has thin evidence. The one hardware masking design provided is validated by static timing analysis and theoretical side-channel assessment, not by measured attacks on a device.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract states timing and 'theoretical' assessments only. It uses promotional language ('truly revolutionary') and claims masking has no effect on speed, with no practical leakage test. The paper has no citations yet and is a single-conference abstract. This is an evidence gap, not proof of weakness.

findings.claim: Systematization work says parts of PQC implementations remain unexplored by existing attack and defense research. The true residual attack surface is therefore not yet mapped.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single SoK abstract. 'Unexplored' means a research gap, not a demonstrated flaw, but it limits confidence in the security of deployed implementations.
findings.supporting_excerpt: highlights unexplored parts in current implementations.

hype_flags: 'Quantum-safe' framing: the abstracts show algorithm-level quantum resistance does not ensure implementation-level security against side-channel and fault attacks.
'Truly revolutionary' ML-DSA masked hardware (src_7aa2585552): support is timing analysis and theoretical assessment, with no measured attack resistance.
Claims that masking solves leakage: a preprint reports higher-order masked FPGA designs still leaked enough for key recovery.
Standardized (NIST-selected) status read as implementation security: the standardized Kyber/ML-KEM is the target of multiple attack papers.

finding.claim: S1 generalises to "constrained" and "IoT-class" hardware and to ML-KEM/ML-DSA being as efficient as elliptic-curve cryptography. The cited abstract covers only Raspberry Pi 1, Zero and 4 and a laptop, all running OpenSSL 3.5. These are Linux-capable single-board computers, not microcontroller-class devices. The abstract does not say the implementations were side-channel protected, so the efficiency parity probably applies to unprotected code. Masked implementations carry extra cost (see R1-R3). The result also rests on one preprint.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quoted hardware set shows the claim's scope is narrower than "constrained hardware". The point about protected implementations is an inference: the abstract is silent on side-channel countermeasures, and the energy cost of masking is not benchmarked. It is a single preprint with no replication shown.
finding.supporting_excerpt: from the 32-bit Raspberry Pi 1 and Zero to the 64-bit Raspberry Pi 4, as well as commodity laptop hardware. Using the FNIRSI FNB58 USB power meter and OpenSSL~3.5
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 names migration as the 'main practical blocker', but the cited abstracts do not rank blockers. src_7af56bdfd5 only says it discusses 'challenges of transitioning', and src_9d1161e3bc offers implications for practitioners. Meanwhile the risk evidence shows implementation-security problems (side-channel leakage, no hardware-agnostic countermeasures) are a documented blocker for the standardised algorithms. These are absent from the Science findings S1-S11, so the 'rather than the existence of candidate algorithms' framing understates the open problems.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows implementation security is named as a challenge. The 'repeatedly named' ranking in S11 is not supported by abstracts that mention transition only in passing. The omission is a general gap: practical readiness is presented as a deployment-logistics problem only.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Some of the identified challenges include the lack of hardware agnostic countermeasures, hardware specific vulnerabilities.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 says the surveys 'consistently' describe five families (lattice, code, hash, multivariate, isogeny). Only src_4f617d8a3a lists all five. src_4aefcdcced mentions only lattice and hash. src_7af56bdfd5 is a three-KEM comparison, and the src_518c5be7fe abstract excerpt does not enumerate families. The 'consistent across surveys' claim is therefore stronger than the retrieved abstracts allow. S8's 'more recently energy consumption' trend rests on a single preprint (src_9d1161e3bc). Both findings describe the retrieved sample rather than the field.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Comparing the cited abstracts shows only one lists all five families, and only one deals with energy. Abstracts alone cannot confirm consistency across the full papers, and the sample is small and retrieval-biased.

finding.claim: S3 mixes two things. The 2022 announcement of four candidates (three lattice, one hash) differs from the finalised standards S1 cites, which are three FIPS documents with two lattice-based and one hash-based. 'Predominantly lattice' is a reading of the 2022 announcement, not a description of the standards now in force. The findings also do not discuss the monoculture risk of leaning on one mathematical family, which side-channel work shows is attacked across several lattice KEMs.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt says 'four possible standards' announced in 2022, not the final standards. Lattice concentration as a shared-risk point is an interpretation. src_232ea2a91d says one attack applies to Kyber, Saber, FrodoKEM and NTRU Prime together.
finding.supporting_excerpt: On July 5, 2022, the National Institute of Standards and Technology announced four possible post-quantum cryptography standards, three of them are based on lattice theory and the other one is based on Hash function.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 states that Shor's algorithm renders RSA/DH/ECC insecure, but the cited review makes this conditional on large quantum computers that do not yet exist. The finding drops that condition. Neither S2's 'Q-day approaching' nor S4 gives any evidence on hardware progress or timelines. The 'approaching' framing is the paper's rhetorical opening, so migration urgency is asserted rather than evidenced.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract's argument depends on the development of large quantum computers. S4 reads as a present-tense fact, and S2 is a framing sentence in a benchmarking paper's abstract. Neither paper supplies a timeline or resource estimate. The Shor/Grover algorithmic statements themselves are fine.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The development of large quantum computers will have dire consequences for cryptography.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 and S9 pull in different directions and the findings do not reconcile them. S6 cites one arXiv survey saying quantum cryptography is 'not a viable solution' and that quantum-resistant cryptography is better. S9 and S5 present quantum technologies (device-independent QKD, QKD-PQC hybrids) as useful complements. The S6 conclusion is a single non-peer-reviewed preprint's judgement about 'present limitations'. S9's 'rather than replacements' is not stated in its abstract, which only suggests ways quantum technologies 'might be used'.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quoted 'might be used' is speculative wording and does not say 'complements rather than replacements', so S9's verified_fact label overreaches. S6 is a single-preprint opinion and should not be placed beside S9 as settled.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Then we suggest specific ways in which quantum technologies might be used to enhance cybersecurity in the near future and beyond.

finding.claim: S5 reports 'little additional overhead' for the QKD-PQC system as a verified fact. This is the authors' own claim from an unreviewed preprint. The comparison baseline is QKD with one-time-pad encryption, not a PQC-only deployment. The same abstract's 'one of the most secure communication systems currently available' is promotional and unsubstantiated. It is a single experimental deployment with no independent validation.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the security claim is a suggestion by the authors. The overhead comparison against QKD with one-time-pad encryption says little about practicality versus plain PQC.
finding.supporting_excerpt: we suggest that our design represents one of the most secure communication systems currently available.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

limitations: Analysis uses abstracts only, and three papers (src_209bb0afd3, src_6ed3300d79, src_12391f12e4) have no abstract, so I did not use them for findings.

The set is heavily skewed to side-channel attacks on lattice KEMs. It has nothing on the quantum threat timeline, migration cost, crypto-agility, algorithm cryptanalysis, hybrid deployment, standards fragmentation, or supply chain concentration, so absence of those risks here is a coverage gap.
src_6e27a8f79f (fermion lattice simulation) is off-topic for PQC risk and was not used.

Two key sources (src_fa5311f9b1 and the arXiv-hosted work) are preprints that are not peer reviewed. Several results are lab experiments on specific devices (Cortex-M4, CW305 FPGA) with attacker physical access assumed.
The abstract for src_232ea2a91d is truncated, so its final result numbers are unavailable.
The papers give no quantitative data on real-world exploitation, so I cannot gauge how likely these attacks are outside the lab.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available. Several abstracts are truncated and some papers have no abstract, so claims about what the full papers say could not be checked.
Several challenges rest on the absence of a statement in an abstract (for example, no mention of side-channel protection in the energy benchmark). That does not show the full papers lack it.

The evidence pool is small and skewed toward side-channel risk. I did not search for cryptanalysis of the lattice assumptions, deployment evidence, or quantum-resource estimates, so those risks are not assessed.
I left S10 unchallenged, and I did not challenge S4's Shor/Grover statements, which the abstract supports.
Some paper dates look unusual (for example 2026 dates). I took metadata at face value and did not verify it.

sources.title: Assessing Readiness of Organization for Post-Quantum Cryptography [US20260352575A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods are provided for analyzing and defining the readiness or preparedness of a network infrastructure to transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) operation. In one implementation, a method includes a step of collecting information with respect to a current state of a network infrastructure associated with an organization, wherein the collected information is related to compliance of the network infrastructure with PQC standards. The method further includes a step of calculating a PQC readiness score from the collected information. Next, the method includes displaying, on a User Interface (UI), the PQC readiness score and one or more recommended remediation actions for improving the PQC readiness score.

sources.title: System and Method for Quantum-Safe Transaction Security Using Entangled Photons [US20260352453A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A quantum-safe transaction security system and method using entangled photons for authentication in finance, voting, and IoT. Entangled photon pairs are generated and distributed via a scalable fiber and satellite network with quantum repeaters. Entanglement verification, AI-driven anomaly detection, AES-256 redundant verification, and tamper-proof detectors ensure transaction integrity with 95% fidelity over 50 km.

sources.title: QUANTUM-RESISTANT ATTESTED KEY AND MODEL LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM [US20260352451A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A quantum-resistant system manages the key and model lifecycle of an artificial intelligence model within a trusted execution environment (TEE). A key management engine generates, seals, rotates, and revokes post-quantum keys bound to a hardware-rooted measurement. A secure model update module applies attested changes linking a prior state to a new state. A verifiable fine-tuning module binds, as a single signed unit, digests of training data, gradients, and resulting weights to the measurement. A tamper-evident provenance ledger records the operations and may anchor digests to a public blockchain. The system may mint a self-sovereign agent identity for consumption by a separate orchestration subsystem. Keys, updates, and evidence exist unencrypted only within the TEE and are tamper-evidently bound to the measurement, so an operator cannot alter or suppress them without invalidating the attestation.

sources.title: METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR STRATEGIZING NETWORK MIGRATION IN ADAPTATION TO POST QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY [EP4835707A1]
sources.abstract: With the advancements in quantum computing, transitioning to quantum-safe cryptography is becoming increasingly critical to keep today's network secure. The present disclosure introduces a method for industrial application network migration. This involves formalizing a Harvest Now Decrypt Later (HNDL) adversarial model, finding a risk score of a successful HNDL attack in any network links followed by in any network component. Graph theory and the Markov chain is used for finding out the central network points. The centrality of network points is measured using a centrality score. The central points are the points in the network, compromising those can compromise a significant part of the total network. Finally, a critical score is given to network points based on risk score, centrality score and metadata about the network points. This critical score can be a priority number given to the network points to rank them for migration to quantum safe state.

sources.abstract: Devices, systems, and methods for memory-efficient post-quantum (PQ) cryptography are provided. A method includes generating, by a hardware security module (HSM), a cryptographic seed, storing, by the HSM, the cryptographic seed, receiving, by the HSM and from a cryptographic processor, a request for the cryptographic seed, and responsive to the request, providing, by the HSM and to the cryptographic processor, the cryptographic seed.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR QUANTUM-RESISTANT CRYPTOGRAPHIC REFLECTION ARCHITECTURE FOR DISTRIBUTED-LEDGER TRANSACTION DATA [US20260342601A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A computer-implemented system for quantum-resistant cryptographic protection of distributed-ledger transaction data. Upon close of a transaction block, a reflection generation engine generates N cryptographic reflections, each comprising a multi-component commitment including content, state, temporal, chain anchor, sibling reflection, and algorithm fingerprint components. Reflections are constructed using a heterogeneous set of cryptographic primitives such that no two reflections share identical primitives, and reflections do not contain recoverable transaction data. Each reflection is distributed to a corresponding vault implemented as a cloud storage service, a custodial storage arrangement, a sovereign data facility, or a smart contract repository, each vault operating under a distinct custody and jurisdictional regime. An anomaly-aware multi-factor authentication gate validates retrieval requests. A three-tier verification module supports existence proof, integrity attestation, and forensic recovery modes.

sources.title: POST-QUANTUM CRYPTOGRAPHY USING HIGH-MEMORY MASKED CONVOLUTIONAL CODES WITH DUAL-LAYER ERROR MECHANISMS [WO2026224702A1]
sources.abstract: A cryptographic encryption system for securing communications resistant to quantum computing attacks. The sender processes a plaintext vector by computing a remainder polynomial and appending its coefficients to form an augmented vector, multiplies the augmented vector by a public key derived from a masked convolutional code, and introduces random errors into the resulting ciphertext sufficient to increase cryptanalytic resistance while maintaining decodability, thereby generating an error-injected ciphertext. The recipient recovers the plaintext by applying an inverse permutation to the error-injected ciphertext, generating candidate unmasked vectors by subtracting possible masking vectors, performing polynomial division on constituent polynomials of each candidate to form candidate decoded vectors, applying parallel Viterbi decoding to identify the most likely codeword, transforming the codeword using an inverse transformation matrix, verifying the result using a predetermined error detection polynomial, and extracting the plaintext vector.

sources.title: ACCEPTANCE-CONTROL LAYER FOR VERIFIED AI-GENERATED CODE [US20260339818A1]
sources.abstract: Disclosed is an acceptance-control layer for AI-generated software code, implemented as a system, method, and non-transitory computer-readable medium. A hardware-enforced deployment gate prevents transmission of candidate code outside a trusted execution environment (TEE) until four conditions are simultaneously satisfied: (i) a formal verification engine produces a machine-checkable proof of one or more correctness properties of the candidate code; (ii) a quantum-resistant cryptographic module produces attestation evidence binding the candidate code, the AI agents, and the proof to the hardware-rooted TEE measurement using one or more post-quantum cryptographic algorithms; (iii) a hardware-rooted consensus engine satisfies a policy-defined threshold among a plurality of validators whose eligibility is bound to the hardware-rooted measurement; and (iv) the candidate code, the proof, the attestation evidence, and the consensus decision are recorded in a tamper-evident provenance ledger supporting independent third-party verification.

The modules cooperate to maintain price stability, ensure transparent and fully backed cross-chain circulation, enable creator monetization, facilitate mainstream payment integration, and provide consumer loyalty rewards, thereby addressing known shortcomings of existing single-asset or algorithmic stablecoins on Ethereum and other blockchain networks while extending the stablecoin's utility into everyday commerce.

Leveraging a decentralized infrastructure, cryptographic network protocols, and integrates deferred cryptographic proofs and quantum-resistant encryption to redefine consent validation. This technology disclosed herein introduces a Dynamic Data Transformation Layer (DDTL) that anonymizes and provisions compliant first-party user data for enterprise applications while ensuring secure, ethical data usage. sources.title: Dynamic Multi-Axis Cubit Array (DMAQA) for AI-Optimized Quantum Tensor Computation [CA3268010A1]
sources.abstract: The Dynamic Multi-Axis Qubit Array (DMAQA) is an AI-driven quantum tensor processing system designed to optimize quantum state evolution, tensor network operations, and AIaccelerated computations. DMAQA integrates multi-axis qubit control, deep reinforcement learning for workload balancing, and hybrid quantum-classical execution, making it highly applicable to quantum simulations, AI model training, cryptographic security, and blockchain verification. Key Features: • Multi-Axis Qubit Array for Tensor Evolution – Optimized processing of high-dimensional quantum states for AI-driven computations. • AI-Assisted Workload Balancing – Uses reinforcement learning to dynamically predict and allocate quantum-classical compute resources. • Hybrid Quantum-Classical Execution – Seamlessly distributes tasks across QPUs, GPUs, CPUs, and TPUs, reducing latency and improving performance. • Scalability Beyond 1024 Qubits – Enables large-scale quantum tensor computations, surpassing current 512-qubit limitations. • Post-Quantum Cryptographic Security – Implements SHA-3 hashing, Kyber key exchange, and Dilithium signatures to ensure quantum-resistant blockchain verification. DMAQA improves tensor contractions, minimizes processing bottlenecks, and enables AI-assisted workload redistribution, ensuring high-speed, secure, and energy-efficient quantum-AI computing.

sources.abstract: [0000]    A method may be implemented by a wireless transmit/receive unit (WTRU), including sending, to a network, a protocol data unit (PDU) session establishment request, which may include an indication of a network function (NF) intent and security requirements. NF-specific security policies (NFSSPs) may be received from the network in response to the PDU session establishment request. The NFSSPs may be associated with a target NF instance. The NFSSPs may be determined to be valid NFSSPs based on a signature associated with each of the NFSSPs. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms may be determined based on the valid NFSSPs or WTRU context information. End-to-end communication may be performed with the target NF instance based on the valid NFSSPs using the PQC algorithms. A security monitoring report may be sent to the network and may be based on a WTRU security monitoring report policy for each of the valid NFSSPs.

An API gateway provides quantum-resistant secure communication with a server-side services module comprising a social media engine, an artificial intelligence engine, a finance and trading module, a quantum security module, and a governance module. A distributed node network implements a three-dimensional spherical blockchain architecture to immutably record social activity, financial transactions, governance actions, and security validations. sources.title: OTN ENCRYPTION METHOD AND APPARATUS [WO2026200579A1]
sources.abstract: An OTN encryption method and apparatus, which relate to the technical field of optical communications. The OTN encryption method and apparatus enable an OTN encryption process be quantum-resistant, and reduce the cost. In one implementation, a quantum random number is used as a session key, and the session key is encrypted by means of a preset key. During a subsequent update, the session key is encrypted by means of the preset key and the previously used quantum random number. By using the preset key and a quantum key, the key transmission of an OTN can achieve a certain degree of resistance to quantum attacks. No asymmetric encryption algorithm is used during key interaction, thereby further enhancing the resistance to quantum attacks. In another implementation, a preset key is used to encrypt a public key, and the key used for encrypting the public key is updated per use, so as to improve the transmission security of the public key, thereby further enhancing the resistance to quantum attacks. The method in the embodiments of the present application requires no additional QKD device, thereby reducing the costs.

The project data structure may indicate a sequence or flow of documents and/or document types. The smart drive system may also manage groups of documents and generate documents and group tokens to manage access permissions. The smart drive system may protect these data sources from unauthorized access based on the quantum tokens corresponding to the document, document type, and/or group of documents. The smart drive system may facilitate modifications to the document from other parties, which may represent counteroffers or a negotiation process. sources.title: Anomaly Detection Using Hybrid Neural Network Framework [US20260291963A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A hybrid quantum-classical framework detects anomalies in network data by integrating quantum and classical neural networks. Data acquisition collects user inputs and network traffic, forming a raw dataset preprocessed with SHA3 hashing and SPHINCS+ quantum-safe signatures for integrity. Quantum encoding with BB84 QKD and CNOT gate entanglement secures quantum transfers, while a quantum neural network validates data, normalizes it, and applies amplitude encoding to extract features using variational quantum circuits with RY/RZ gates, optimized via gradient descent. A variational quantum recurrent network with quantum memory classifies anomalies, thresholding scores at 0.9 to generate severity-ranked alerts. A classical convolutional neural network analyzes spatial patterns, with a multi-translation layer fusing quantum and classical outputs. An integration module combines results, adjusts circuit depth, monitors latency, and logs anomalies to persistent storage, ensuring real-time, comprehensive anomaly detection across diverse network environments.

draft.summary: Research and patent activity on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is rising fast. Papers rose from 849 in 2024 to 1,925 in 2025, and 2026 year-to-date is up about 126% on the same point in 2025. Patent publications are also up about 108% year-to-date (S7, S8, P1). The NIST-standardised algorithms ML-KEM and ML-DSA look efficient on Linux-class devices (S1, with the caveats in C1). Cisco and F5 describe PQC features in shipped products or portfolios (M1, M3), and filings from banks and telecoms treat it as a mainstream disclosure topic (M5, M4, M8). The evidence does not show hardware timelines for a quantum computer that breaks current encryption (C5), customer adoption in enterprises, or revenue tied to PQC. Documented side-channel weaknesses in protected ML-KEM hardware (R1-R3) and the migration burden (M2, M5, S11) are the main uncertainties. Many science findings rest on single preprints (C1, C3, C7).
draft.plain_summary: Post-quantum cryptography is a new kind of data-scrambling designed to stay safe even if powerful quantum computers arrive. Research and patent filings are growing quickly, and some networking companies already sell products with it. The main thing that could slow it down is that switching old systems over is hard and the new methods can still leak secrets through the hardware that runs them.

bear.label: forecast
